newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Prices steady, planting proceeds.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Prices steady, planting proceeds.

text.p: Generally firm Australian grain prices slid only slightly last week despite Chicago's fall, as planting continued and prospects for new crop wheat looked good.
Markets were generally quiet while heavy wheat planting continued in the main eastern producing state of New South Wales (NSW).
"Farmers are really focused on getting things planted and it's progressing very well," Guy Allen of NSW handling and trading group GrainCorp said.
"(It's) optimum planting weather across the state and prices are weaker on good conditions as well as lower export markets."

Most of the north and north-west of NSW was looking good with new crop planting, Bill Mitchell of Armidale-based New England Agricultural Traders (NEAT), in the state's central-north grainbelt, also said.

Southern parts of NSW and further south into the state of Victoria still need more rain, but Western Australia (WA), which last season produced almost as much wheat as NSW, has had reasonable rainfall in its grains-growing areas.

A weather official with the WA Bureau of Meteorology told Reuters on Friday that good April rain in the state's grain areas had been followed in the past week or so with falls of five to 10 millimetres in many grain-growing areas.
Some places had received up to 20 mm, while in south and southwest coastal regions falls were up to 50 mm.
"Some areas are saying we need more rain and others are saying turn it off," he said.

Australia seemed to have scored another big export order last week in a 378,000 tonne sale of white wheat for June/July delivery to Pakistan at US$171.00-$172.00 a tonne fob, according to trade reports.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) on Friday could not officially confirm the sale, although the deal appears done.
Australian domestic markets were quiet last week.
Generally steady futures prices were accompanied by light trade in old crop cash wheat, which slipped by A$5.00-A$8.00 to A$185.00-A$187.00 delivered Newcastle, on Allen's book.
New crop cash wheat edged back by A$2.00-A$3.00 to about A$165.00 delivered Newcastle.
Sorghum fell by A$1.00-A$2.00 to about A$160.00 Newcastle.
Allen noted that the weaker Australian dollar helped local prices stay firm.
"It's been dreadfully quiet," said NEAT's Mitchell, who believes U.S. wheat is reaching for its floor price given this season's fair supply outlook.
Australian wheat's refusal to fall as far as U.S. wheat reflected some local belief in that view, he said. Supplies were still tight, he noted.
The AWB's steady estimated 1997/98 pool price range of A$190.00-A$200.00 a tonne was also helping support the local market, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
